pm8_laws.topic: State laws against boycotts of Israel

claims.text: As of 2024, 38 US states had passed bills or executive orders discouraging boycotts of Israel; Illinois (SB 1761, signed 23 July 2015) was the first to explicitly punish them; in 2015 the Israel Allies Foundation drafted a model act combining the South Carolina and Illinois bills; AIPAC, the Israel Action Network and local Jewish federations lobbied for the laws, and a lobbyist for the Israeli-American Council drafted or pushed bills in several states.

The laws are of two kinds: contract laws requiring government contractors to certify they do not boycott Israel (some exempting small contracts) and investment laws requiring public funds to avoid or divest from boycotting entities, with blacklists kept by states including Arizona, Florida, Illinois, Indiana and Colorado.

Courts have divided: in Kansas (Koontz v. Watson) a preliminary injunction issued and the law was amended in 2018; in Texas (Amawi v. Pflugerville ISD) a federal court found HB 89 unconstitutional in April 2019; in Arizona (Jordahl) an injunction issued in 2018 and the law was amended; in Arkansas the Eighth Circuit en banc upheld Act 710 in June 2022 on the ground that boycott purchasing decisions are not protected expression, and the Supreme Court denied review on 21 February 2023.

The Arkansas Times, which said it was not boycotting Israel, refused on principle to sign the certification in 2018 to renew an advertising contract with Pulaski Technical College; the ACLU argued the law penalizes one side of a political debate.

No federal anti-BDS law has been adopted: the Israel Anti-Boycott Act (2017) died; the Combating BDS Act (S. 1) passed the Senate in January 2019 but not the House; the House passed a non-binding resolution against BDS in July 2019, 398–17.

pm8_bonds.topic: State and local money in Israel Bonds

claims.text: US states and municipalities bought more than $1.7 billion of Israeli government bonds from October 2023 to July 2024; Israel Bonds (the Development Corporation for Israel, launched 1951, the SEC-registered underwriter selling for Israel's Finance Ministry) has raised $52 billion in seven decades.

Palm Beach County, Florida, announced $160M more in October 2023, raised its cap from 10% to 15% of its portfolio in March 2024 and by April held about $700M of a $4.67B portfolio, calling itself the world's largest Israel Bonds investor; Florida held more than $250M; Ohio's treasurer bought $357.5M since 2019, including $20M announced on 11 October 2023; Pennsylvania's holdings reached $56M.

Israel Bonds courted state officials with trips to Israel, awards and conferences that paid speakers' expenses; three Palm Beach County residents sued in May 2024 alleging investment for political reasons; DAWN asked the Justice Department whether Israel Bonds should register as a foreign agent, which it denies; Israel Bonds calls its marketing legitimate and common practice and says Israel has never missed a payment.
